SUBJECT

Put rules around open slots

PREVIEW

Set notice, time-blocking, and meeting-volume boundaries for link-booked calls.

Hi there,

A scheduling link can follow rules, not just expose open slots. SavvyCal is online meeting scheduling software that lets you set those rules around link-booked calls.

Minimum Notice requires lead time before a new event. Time Blocking lets SavvyCal honor calendar events you use to budget your time.

Buffers & Limits can also cap meeting quantity by day, week, or month. Your calendar gets a vote before another call lands on it.

An account gives you a place to try these controls against the boundaries you want for client, partner, and investor calls—and decide whether they fit your week.

Create your SavvyCal account → https://savvycal.com/

- the SavvyCal team

#1 “Put rules around open slots”

AI assessment, not a performance forecast

6/10

Selected proposition

Calendar-protection controls are a separate, well-supported reason for a founder managing their own week to evaluate SavvyCal, especially when the concern is booking volume or calls landing too close to important meetings rather than the social feel of the link.

Decision: Decide whether SavvyCal's notice, time-blocking, and meeting-volume controls fit the boundaries the founder wants around link-booked calls.

Next step: Creating an account provides a path to evaluate Minimum Notice, honored time blocks, and day, week, or month meeting caps against the founder's own scheduling rules.

Destination: /signup

Limits: This evaluation does not establish that SavvyCal can rank or restrict availability according to who the booker is.

What they thought you were selling

SavvyCal is scheduling software that would let me keep sending a booking link while enforcing advance notice, protected calendar blocks, buffers, and meeting-count limits.

Situation recognition: The profile establishes that I personally send one scheduling link for client, partner, and investor meetings and feel uneasy doing it. The email addresses control over link-booked calls, so the category is relevant. But it assumes that insufficient notice, ignored time blocks, or excessive meeting volume is my current problem; the profile does not establish any of those. It also does not address the stated discomfort about how sending the link comes across.

Importance now: Controlling a public booking link is plausibly useful, but the profile only establishes that I wince when sending the link, not that meeting volume or calendar-boundary violations are hurting me now. The email therefore addresses a possible operational risk while leaving my explicitly established social discomfort untouched.

Assumed: Profile-supported: I personally send a scheduling link for client, partner, and investor calls.; Email-only: people are booking with too little notice.; Email-only: I use calendar events to budget or protect my time.; Email-only: link-booked meetings exceed a daily, weekly, or monthly quantity I would want to permit.; Email-only: exposing open slots without additional rules is causing enough disruption to justify changing scheduling software.

“I would have clicked if this email had told me…”

I would have clicked if this email had told me the price or trial terms and approximately how long it takes to test these rules with my existing calendar and booking workflow.

What stopped them

I do not know whether creating an account means a quick, reversible trial or a time-consuming switch from my current scheduling setup, and the email gives me no price, trial terms, or setup-effort signal. Three minutes before a meeting, that is enough uncertainty to postpone the click.

Lines they would cut or change

— Rewrite "A scheduling link can follow rules, not just expose open slots." as "If your public booking link is fragmenting your week, SavvyCal lets you require notice, protect time blocks, and cap how many calls can be booked." This makes the problem conditional instead of assuming I have it.
— Cut "Your calendar gets a vote before another call lands on it." The preceding sentence already explains the feature, and this line adds metaphor when I am scanning quickly.
— Rewrite "An account gives you a place to try these controls against the boundaries you want for client, partner, and investor calls—and decide whether they fit your week." to state the concrete trial commitment: whether payment is required, what calendar access is needed, and roughly how long the test takes.
— Rewrite "Create your SavvyCal account →" as a smaller, explicit next step such as "See pricing and how the rules work →" unless account creation is genuinely free and reversible, in which case say that directly.

What they thought you were selling

SavvyCal is scheduling software that would let me keep using a booking link while enforcing notice periods, calendar time blocks, buffers, and meeting-volume limits.

Situation recognition: The profile establishes that I personally send one scheduling link for client, partner, and investor meetings, so controlling that link is relevant. It does not establish that short-notice or excessive bookings currently disrupt my week, and the email does not test that premise; applicability is therefore unknown rather than false.

Importance now: Protecting time around a public booking link is a plausible and relevant risk, but the profile does not establish that uncontrolled bookings are an urgent problem this Tuesday morning.

Assumed: Profile-supported: I personally send a scheduling link for business meetings.; Email-only: link-booked calls are landing without enough notice.; Email-only: bookings disregard calendar blocks I use to budget my time.; Email-only: I need daily, weekly, or monthly meeting caps.; Email-only: I am willing to create an account to evaluate a replacement or additional scheduling tool.

“I would have clicked if this email had told me…”

I would have clicked if this email had told me the exact time and commitment required to test one link, including whether a free trial is available and whether I must replace my current setup.

What stopped them

Creating an account sounds like setup work, but the email does not tell me whether I can test this quickly, what it costs, or whether I would need to replace my current booking link and reconnect my calendar.

— Rewrite “Create your SavvyCal account →” to name the immediate commitment, such as “See how the rules work” or, if supported, “Test one booking link free—no card required.”

What they thought you were selling

SavvyCal is scheduling software that would let me keep using booking links while enforcing notice periods, protected calendar blocks, and limits on how many meetings can land in my week.

Situation recognition: The profile establishes that I personally send one public booking link to clients, partners, and investors, so rules that protect time across those requests are relevant. The email does not establish that I currently suffer excessive bookings or displaced high-priority meetings, so the urgency is uncertain; it also does not address the explicitly established discomfort I feel when sending the link.

Importance now: Protecting my week from poorly timed or excessive bookings is a plausible risk because one link serves several kinds of contacts, but the profile does not establish that this is causing a problem this Tuesday. The discomfort I do have now—pasting a scheduling link in business conversations—is not directly resolved by the email.

Assumed: Profile-supported: I personally send a scheduling link for client, partner, and investor meetings.; Email-only: I need more minimum notice before link-booked calls.; Email-only: calendar events I use to budget time are not already protected adequately.; Email-only: meeting volume is high enough that daily, weekly, or monthly caps would help.; Email-only: creating another scheduling account is an acceptable way to test these controls.

“I would have clicked if this email had told me…”

I would have clicked if this email had told me I could test these rules free with my existing calendar and booking link before changing my workflow.

What stopped them

I cannot tell how much setup or commitment this trial requires—especially whether I can test it with my current calendar and booking workflow without paying or replacing anything first.

Lines they would cut or change

— Rewrite “Time Blocking lets SavvyCal honor calendar events you use to budget your time.” as “Mark focus time or other calendar events as unavailable, even when the slot would otherwise look open.”
— Rewrite “An account gives you a place to try these controls against the boundaries you want for client, partner, and investor calls—and decide whether they fit your week.” to state the concrete trial terms, required calendar connection, and whether I must replace my current booking link.
— Rewrite “Create your SavvyCal account →” as a lower-commitment CTA that accurately names the first step, such as testing the rules, if that option is actually available.
